document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most frequent malignancy in white populations. European multidisciplinary experts updated guidance on its diagnosis and treatment and distinguish ‘easy-to-treat’ from ‘difficult-to-treat’ BCC using the EADO clinical classification. Clinical and dermatoscopic findings generally establish the diagnosis, but uncertain lesions require histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical removal is first-line treatment. Micrographically controlled surgery shall be offered for high-risk or recurrent tumours and those at critical anatomical sites. Topical or destructive treatments can be considered for low-risk superficial BCC; photodynamic therapy is effective for superficial and low-risk nodular BCC. A multidisciplinary tumour board should discuss difficult-to-treat cases. Patients with locally advanced or metastatic BCC should be offered the Hedgehog inhibitors vismodegib or sonidegib. Anti-PD1 treatment with cemiplimab is a second-line option after progression, contraindication or intolerance to Hedgehog inhibitors. Radiotherapy is an alternative when surgery is unsuitable or declined, particularly in older patients; electrochemotherapy may be offered if surgery or radiotherapy is contraindicated. Gorlin syndrome requires regular skin examinations for early detection and treatment. Long-term follow-up is recommended for high-risk BCC, multiple BCCs and Gorlin syndrome.

document_sections.heading: 1. Information about the guidelines
document_sections.content: This European interdisciplinary consensus guideline updates recommendations for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of BCC.

document_sections.heading: 1.4. Scope
document_sections.content: The guideline is intended to support clinicians caring for people with BCC. Its update responds particularly to a new clinical classification and developments in non-invasive diagnostic imaging, electrochemotherapy and immunotherapy for difficult-to-treat disease. Its intended clinical effect is improved patient care.

document_sections.heading: 1.5. Target population
document_sections.content: Recommendations address diagnosis, treatment and follow-up throughout the BCC spectrum, including common, difficult-to-treat and advanced tumours.

document_sections.heading: 1.6. Objectives
document_sections.content: The principal audience is clinicians managing BCC. The classification reflects complex clinical situations rather than relying solely on a sequential prognostic model such as TNM, which is less readily applicable to BCC. The guideline emphasises non-invasive imaging, systemic targeted treatment and immunotherapy for advanced disease, and briefly addresses prevention.

document_sections.heading: 1.7. Audience and period of validity
document_sections.content: The guidance supports evidence-based care but does not replace nationally accepted guidelines. Conclusions reflect evidence available when it was prepared and may change with future research; individual circumstances can justify different management. An update is anticipated approximately every 3 years, with an expiry date of December 2026, or earlier if medical advances warrant it.

document_sections.heading: 1.8. Principles of methodology
document_sections.content: This is an update of the 2019 European consensus guideline, also informed by other contemporary guidelines, including NCCN version 1.2023 and the British Association of Dermatologists 2021 guideline. Authors searched English-language Medline publications through 15th March 2023. Development followed AGREE II standards, using the best available evidence and good clinical practice (GCP). Evidence levels follow the Oxford classification, whose question-specific study-design categories are shown in Table 1. Its notes allow downgrading for study quality, imprecision, indirectness, inconsistency or a very small absolute effect, and upgrading for a large or very large effect; a systematic review is generally preferable to an individual study. Recommendation grades are A, a strong recommendation expressed as ‘shall’; B, a recommendation expressed as ‘should’; C, a weak recommendation expressed as ‘may/can’; X, an intervention that should not be recommended; and 0, a pending recommendation where evidence is unavailable or insufficient either for or against it. Expert consensus supplements areas without adequate evidence.

document_sections.heading: 1.9. Consensus-building process
document_sections.content: Experts involved in national guideline development prepared an initial draft; specialists representing EADO, EDF, ESTRO, UEMS and EADV then contributed. At the Rome consensus meeting on 25th November 2022, 32 experts approved the text, and recommendations in structured boxes and the algorithm required agreement of at least 80%. Voting permitted agreement, disagreement or abstention and comments. Coauthors finalised the draft and recommendations by email in April 2023.

document_sections.heading: 2. Definition
document_sections.content: BCC is a carcinoma of epidermal origin and the most frequent human malignancy. Its name reflects the resemblance of cells at the edge of tumour nests to epidermal basal cells; it is now thought to arise from hair-follicle stem cells. It usually develops on sun-exposed skin in fair-skinned individuals, most often on the head or neck. With chronic sun exposure as the principal carcinogen, incidence rises in older people and peaks at around 80 years of age. The usual lesion is a slowly enlarging, skin-coloured, shiny pearly nodule with surface arborising vessels; larger lesions can ulcerate centrally. Superficial BCC (sBCC) commonly affects the trunk and is associated mainly with intermittent sun exposure. Other presentations include pigmented or sclerosing tumours. Fewer than 1% of patients develop metastases, but delayed detection, inadequate management or neglect can allow extensive, locally advanced and deeply infiltrative disease.

document_sections.heading: 3. Epidemiology
document_sections.content: BCC represents about 75% of keratinocyte cancers, and the estimated lifetime risk in white-skinned people is approximately 30%. Incidence is difficult to establish because routine registration and histopathological assessment are incomplete and registries often record only a patient's first confirmed BCC. Reported increases across countries are associated with changing sun exposure and population ageing; estimates also vary by latitude, study period and registration method. Australia has the highest reported incidence, followed by the United States and Europe. Northern European incidence rises with age, more markedly in women; increases over time have been relatively greater among younger people, especially women. Swedish registry data from 2004 to 2017 showed an increase in age-standardised person-based incidence from 308 per 100,000 in 2004 to 405 per 100,000 in 2017, with aggressive subtypes apparently increasing faster. A Netherlands study reported annual incidence decreases of 3.6% in males and 3.0% in females aged 30–39 years, but a continuing upward trend at ≥50 years. The stated 10-year projections are 30-4% for males and 25-3% for females. A qualitative systematic review found no significant difference in all-cause mortality risk for people with previous BCC. After a first BCC, the risk of another BCC rises substantially, as does the less frequent risk of SCC or melanoma; this varies geographically. High-frequency BCC (HF-BCC), occurring in a very small proportion without the germline mutations or phenotype of a genetic syndrome, is defined as ≥9 BCCs over a 3-year period. It is associated with male sex and previous SCC or melanoma; affected patients also have increased risks of lymphoma, leukaemia, breast cancer and colon cancer. Advanced BCC comprises locally advanced BCC (laBCC) and metastatic BCC (mBCC). A retrospective US cohort attributed 0.8% of BCC cases to laBCC, with an age-adjusted incidence of 1.83 per 100,000 persons and a projection of 4399 US cases; advanced disease rates were highest in males and those older than 65 years. Estimated incidence of histologically confirmed mBCC is 0.0028–0.55%. A tertiary-centre retrospective analysis classified 0.6% of BCCs as severe, encompassing disease unsuitable for surgery or radiotherapy, metastatic disease or disease requiring extensive treatment. The true incidence, prevalence and mortality of mBCC remain underestimated because staging was previously uncommon and advanced-disease registries are recent.

document_sections.heading: 4. Aetiology and genetics
document_sections.content: The proposed cellular origin of BCC remains debated: many tumours appear to arise from hair-follicle stem cells, whereas another view places their stem cells in interfollicular epidermis or the infundibulum. Different carcinogens may act on different stem-cell compartments. Difficulty establishing BCC cell lines suggests that unknown environmental or cellular factors support their isolation and growth. Ultraviolet light (UV) is the main carcinogen. BCC has a tumour mutational burden (TMB) of 65 mutations/megabases, compared with 14 mutations/megabases for melanoma, and many UV-signature C:T or CC:TT transitions at dipyrimidine sites. Indoor tanning is associated with greater skin-cancer risk, including BCC, in a dose-response relationship. Other environmental causes include ionising radiation and arsenic; fair skin, red hair, blue eyes, older age and immunodeficiency, including treatment-related immunosuppression, HIV and haematological malignancy, are additional factors. MC1R variants affect pigmentation and are associated with sporadic BCC risk, OR (95% confidence interval [CI]) 1.39 (1.15–1.69). Most BCCs are sporadic. Hedgehog (Hh) pathway activation is the principal genetic driver: inactivating PTCH1 mutations on chromosome 9q22.3 occur in about 90% of sporadic cases and activating SMO mutations in approximately 10%. Hh alterations also occur in medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma, which may affect people with Gorlin syndrome. This syndrome predisposes to multiple BCCs through germline PTCH1 mutations or, less often, PTCH2, SMO or SUFU mutations. A small proportion of BCCs lack Hh-pathway mutations. Other reported alterations involve MYCN, PPP6C, STK19, LATS1, ERBB2, PIK23C, N-RAS, K-RAS, HRAS, PTPN14, RB1, FBXW7 and P53; no genetic profile has yet been linked to a particular histopathological subtype. Hippo-pathway changes include increased YAP1 and Taz. Primary Hedgehog inhibitor (HHI) resistance may involve non-canonical Hh signalling or other pathways; resistant tumours have been reported to share SMO and MYCN mutations with secondarily resistant tumours, extensive rearrangement and Hippo-Yap and WNT activation. Secondary resistance can involve SMO mutations affecting drug binding or activation, or SUFU and Gli2 copy-number changes. Reduced TAP-1 and MHC-I expression, fewer infiltrating CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, more T-regs and effects of IL-10 and Th2 cytokines contribute to low BCC immunogenicity. Table 2 compares frequent BCC-associated genodermatoses, their genes, inheritance and clinical features: xeroderma pigmentosum, Gorlin syndrome, Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome, oculocutaneous albinism and Muir–Torre syndrome. Xeroderma pigmentosum involves germline nucleotide-excision repair defects and can produce early multiple BCCs, melanoma and cutaneous SCC. Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome is X-linked dominant, features follicular atrophoderma, congenital hypotrichosis, hypohidrosis, facial milia and multiple BCCs, and is associated with chromosome Xq26.1 duplications likely to dysregulate ARHGAP36. Other associated rare disorders include Oley and Rombo syndromes, Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome, Bloom, Werner and Rothmund–Thomson syndromes, cartilage-hair hypoplasia, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, and Cowden and Schöpf–Schulz–Passarge syndromes.

document_sections.heading: 5. New EADO classification and staging: common and difficult-to-treat BCC
document_sections.content: BCC commonly grows slowly from a small papule into a nodule or plaque, sometimes ulcerated. Recognised forms include superficial, nodular, morpheic and ulcerated (ulcus rodens), but common tumours do not always fit neatly into these categories. Calling BCC indolent is warranted only when it is treated promptly and adequately: local destruction and invasion can occur despite rare metastasis. Years without treatment or repeated postsurgical relapse can produce locally advanced disease. Although ‘advanced’ has no precise definition, it generally denotes prolonged untreated disease or repeated treatment failure or recurrence, extensive adjacent tissue destruction, and difficulty or inability to cure with standard surgery or radiotherapy. The EADO scheme distinguishes common ‘easy-to-treat’ from ‘difficult-to-treat’ BCC. More than 90% are initially easy to manage with standard surgery or alternative treatments without margin control. Difficult-to-treat disease includes all laBCC and otherwise common tumours complicated by size or location that threatens function or appearance, indistinct margins, repeated facial recurrence, prior radiotherapy, unwillingness to accept surgery or interfering comorbidity. Its five practical groups are: common tumours rendered difficult by tumour- or patient-related circumstances; difficulty due to lesion number; large or destructive disease away from critical sites; large or destructive disease at critical or functional sites; and giant or deeply invasive disease involving extracutaneous tissue. Fig. 1 depicts this classification and staging. Because BCC does not generally progress through tumour, nodal and distant-metastatic steps, TNM is considered irrelevant here. The EADO four-stage scheme places most easy-to-treat low-risk BCC in EADO-stage I; difficult-to-treat common tumours in stage IIA and cases difficult because of lesion number in stage IIB; large destructive tumours away from critical areas in stage IIIA, at critical or functional areas in stage IIIB, and extremely destructive tumours in stage IIIC; and metastatic BCC in stage IV. Its prognostic value remains unproven and needs prospective evaluation. Progression-free or overall survival curves are not considered meaningful for these often RECIST-unmeasurable tumours, which may destroy substantial anatomy without changing survival.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Definition of low- and high-risk BCC
document_sections.content: Recurrence risk provides another low- versus high-risk classification. All difficult-to-treat tumours are high risk, largely because management constraints can compromise optimal treatment or excision margins. Most easy-to-treat tumours are low risk, but apparently straightforward lesions may remain high risk if they affect the facial H area, have perineural or perivascular involvement, or occur in immunosuppressed patients. BCC treated by ablation without histopathological control rather than excision could also be considered high risk. Consequences of recurrence differ: recurrent invasive disease on eyelids, nose, lips or ears can be substantially harmful, whereas recurrent superficial disease on the back is readily managed.

document_sections.heading: 6. Diagnosis 6.1. Clinical and dermatoscopic diagnosis
document_sections.content: BCC usually appears as a slowly enlarging pink or reddish, pearly or translucent papule, plaque or nodule with arborising surface vessels. It may be brown, black or blue, can eventually ulcerate centrally, and infiltrative or morpheic disease may resemble a flat or atrophic scar. In a diagnostic systematic review, unaided examination had sensitivity 66.9% and specificity 97.2%; adding dermatoscopy raised these to 85.0% and 98.2%. Pooled dermatoscopy sensitivity and specificity were 91.2% and 95.0%, with better performance for pigmented disease, expert assessment and in-person examination rather than photographs. Dermatoscopy particularly assists differentiation from melanoma, SCC, Bowen’s disease and benign lesions; equivocal subtype assessment requires histopathology. BCC dermatoscopic findings include arborising or superficial branching vessels, erosions, ulceration, blue-grey clods, leaf-like and spoke-wheel patterns, concentric structures and white structureless findings. Aggregated yellow-white globules have also been described, especially in high-risk head-and-neck subtypes; individuals with multiple tumours may show a recurring personal pattern. A review of 31 studies and 5950 BCCs found arborising vessels in 59%, shiny white structures in 49% and large blue–grey ovoid nests in 34%, with frequencies differing by subtype. Nodular BCC is typically a skin-coloured to reddish, sometimes translucent lesion on the head or neck with prominent focused arborising vessels; pigmented examples can have blue-grey clods. Superficial BCC generally forms a well-defined scaly red patch or plaque on the trunk or lower limbs, often with multiple lesions. Its dermatoscopic findings include pale or pink-red structureless areas, small erosions and fine peripheral vessels; pigmentation can produce leaf-like, spoke-wheel and concentric structures, while polarised dermatoscopy may show short white lines. Blue-grey clods and branching linear vessels argue against the superficial subtype. Morpheic BCC is a poorly demarcated reddish plaque or scar-like area, generally showing white structureless areas and fine arborising vessels without usual ulceration. Basosquamous carcinoma commonly presents as an ulcerated facial nodule or plaque in older photodamaged men and may combine dermatoscopic BCC and invasive SCC features, including peripheral arborising vessels, keratin, white areas, scale, ulceration, crust, blue-grey blotches and blood spots within keratin. Clinical examination supported by dermatoscopy can establish typical small nodular disease of the head, neck or trunk, superficial disease of trunk or limbs, or multiple lesions in Gorlin syndrome without histology. Facial lesions that raise concern or features suggesting aggressive disease warrant biopsy and histopathology. Dermatoscopy also helps predict subtype before surgery and assess response to topical treatment. Table 3 relates individual dermatoscopic signs to their appearances and associated subtypes. Box 1 permits clinical examination assisted by non-invasive methods for superficial and nodular BCC without mandatory histology (Grade of recommendation C; Level of evidence 3; consensus 100%). Box 2 states that dermatoscopy increases clinical diagnostic accuracy (Grade of recommendation A; Level of evidence 1; consensus 100%). Fig. 2 illustrates dermatoscopic criteria.

document_sections.heading: 6.2. Other non-invasive imaging techniques
document_sections.content: Reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM), optical coherence tomography (OCT) and line-field confocal (LC)-OCT can aid diagnosis when dermatoscopy is equivocal, although access is often limited to specialist centres. A meta-analysis estimated RCM sensitivity at 0.97 (95% CI, 0.90–0.99) and specificity at 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88–0.96). A prospective randomised multicentre study found in vivo RCM non-inferior to punch-biopsy-based standard care for diagnosis and subtype assessment before BCC surgery; RCM has also monitored nonsurgical treatment of superficial and genodermatosis-associated multiple BCC. OCT can rapidly assess deep and lateral margins across a large field and may help select surgical versus nonsurgical care. A meta-analysis found improved sensitivity and specificity over visual inspection plus dermatoscopy for challenging lesions. A prospective multicentre study reported 97.8% BCC detection; biopsy-free subtyping was possible in 44% of patients, with predictive values of 84.3% for sBCC and 98.8% for non-sBCC. A multicentre randomised trial found OCT-guided BCC diagnosis non-inferior to conventional punch biopsy. Combined RCM and OCT may assist diagnosis, depth and margin assessment and identification of infiltrative features before Mohs micrographic surgery. LC-OCT combines cellular resolution to 400 μm of depth with OCT-like 3-Dimaging and vertical and horizontal views. Retrospective studies report agreement with histopathology for presurgical subtype assessment and usefulness when monitoring imiquimod-treated sBCC. Box 3 says RCM and/or OCT shall be used when accessible to increase diagnostic accuracy in difficult-to-recognise BCC (Grade of recommendation A; Level of evidence 1; consensus 100%).

document_sections.heading: 6.3. Histopathological diagnosis
document_sections.content: Histopathology is required for uncertain lesions, uncertain large or ulcerated tumours and high-risk BCC, including assessment of excision margins. Multiple biopsies are recommended for laBCC subtype confirmation. In low-risk disease, non-invasive imaging may suffice, particularly before topical or destructive therapy. Incisional biopsy is indicated when recurrence after surgery or topical or destructive treatment is suspected in low-risk subtypes. Box 4 requires histopathological confirmation for equivocal lesions, ulcerated or large tumours, and BCC at high-risk sites (Grade of recommendation B; Level of evidence 3; consensus 100%). In the WHO classification, lower-recurrence-risk histological subtypes are nodular, superficial, pigmented, infundibulocystic and fibroepithelial; higher-risk types are basosquamous carcinoma, sclerosing/morpheic, infiltrating, sarcomatoid-differentiated and micronodular BCC. Mixed forms and collision tumours with SCC occur. Ber-EP4 supports BCC identification and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) supports SCC identification, particularly for difficult differential diagnoses, micrographic margins and distinction from benign follicular hyperplasia. An expert position paper proposes grouping sclerosing, infiltrating and micronodular forms as an ‘infiltrative’ subtype. Pathology reports should document subtype, lateral and deep margin status, and whether perineural and angiolymphatic invasion are present.

document_sections.heading: 7. Staging work up
document_sections.content: Initial evaluation should include a detailed history and examination of all skin because additional keratinocyte carcinomas and melanoma are more likely after BCC. Low-risk disease does not need imaging. For advanced disease, a multidisciplinary team should select imaging according to tumour site and suspected local, regional or metastatic spread. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred for suspected soft-tissue or perineural extension; Computed tomography with or without contrast is preferred for suspected bone involvement.

document_sections.heading: 8. Management of common (easy-to-treat and difficultto-treat) BCC
document_sections.content: Treatment is selected according to tumour characteristics, recurrence risk and patient circumstances. Fig. 3 presents the EADO treatment algorithm, including surgical and nonsurgical options.

document_sections.heading: 8.1. Surgery
document_sections.content: Most primary BCCs can be treated surgically; selected subtypes permit nonsurgical treatment. Larger size, facial H-zone location, aggressive histology, prior recurrence and prolonged immunosuppression increase recurrence risk. Locally destructive or otherwise difficult cases may need multidisciplinary review. Excision may use standard 2D margins or staged micrographically controlled 3D assessment. Reported recurrence after surgery ranges from < 1% to 8% at 5 years, with the best outcomes for micrographically controlled approaches. For low-risk lesions when surgery is unsuitable or impractical, destructive treatments, topical agents or photodynamic therapy (PDT) can be used, although treatment failure is more likely than after excision. Topical and destructive approaches do not permit examination of the destroyed tissue; limited penetration, including with PDT, may leave deeper tumour, while deeper cryotherapy can produce unacceptable scarring. Methods without margin control should generally be avoided when deep invasion, subclinical extension or elevated local-recurrence risk cannot be excluded. Box 5 says surgical excision with subsequent histopathological verification shall be offered as standard BCC care (Grade of recommendation A; Level of evidence 1; consensus 100%). Box 6 allows topical or destructive treatment to be considered for low-risk superficial or nodular BCC when a patient declines surgery or cannot undergo it (GCP; consensus 100%).

document_sections.heading: 8.1.1. Standard excision with 2D histology
document_sections.content: Excision aims to remove visible BCC and microscopic extension in surrounding apparently normal skin, taking a peripheral safety margin. Standard 2D histology usually examines vertical sections of fixed, embedded tissue. Box 7 recommends 3–4 mm safety margins for low-risk BCC undergoing standard 2D excision (GCP; consensus 100%). Box 8 says high-risk BCC should receive at least 5 mm where anatomy permits (GCP; consensus 100%). Guidance cited in the document spans 2 mm to 5 mm for low-risk and 5 mm to 15 mm for high-risk lesions. Size, primary or recurrent status, histological subtype and perineural invasion inform expected subclinical spread. A meta-analysis of 16,066 lesions found that a 3-mm margin achieved a 95% cure rate in non-morpheaform BCC ≤2 cm; a 2 cm tumour with further high-risk factors would require at least 13 mm for comparable certainty of clearance. Studies of clearly demarcated pigmented common BCC reported 99% removal with 2–3 mm margins. Narrower margins may be considered where reconstruction is limited if subsequent reconstruction occurs within 3D-controlled surgery. Cited guidance recommends deep excision to subcutaneous tissue, or to fascia, perichondrium or periosteum for head lesions. Dermatoscopy, RCM, OCT and LC-OCT have been studied for defining margins beyond visible tumour, especially for non-pigmented, poorly defined BCC, but routine implementation needs more research.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.2. Re-excision after histologically narrow margins
document_sections.content: Visible and microscopic margins need not coincide because clinically hidden tumour can extend into the safety margin and excised tissue shrinks during fixation. Expected shrinkage is 17−20% in length and about 10% in width, although older elastotic skin shrinks less. Evidence does not currently support another excision solely because histologically tumour-free margins are narrow. Box 9 states that re-excision is unnecessary when histological margins are clear (GCP; consensus 100%).

document_sections.heading: 8.1.3. Micrographically controlled surgery
document_sections.content: Micrographically controlled 3D surgery examines surgical margins comprehensively through vertical and/or horizontal approaches, supporting complete removal of infiltrative tumours at difficult sites while conserving adjacent tissue. It provides aesthetic outcomes superior or comparable to less reliable nonsurgical methods and is described as efficient, cost-effective and associated with the highest cure rates. In a prospective randomised comparison, primary BCC 10-year cumulative recurrence was 12.2% after standard 2D excision versus 4.4% after micrographically controlled surgery (p = 0.100); corresponding recurrent-BCC figures were 13.5% and 3.9% (p = 0.023). Standard excision can also require more extensive or less cosmetically desirable reconstruction. Stepwise 3D surgery is appropriate, where technically available, for high-risk primary tumours, subclinical extension, aggressive growth or cosmetically or functionally sensitive sites such as the central face. Recurrent tumours should undergo microscopic control: their reported 5-year re-recurrence rate is 11.6% to 17.4%, while a series of 174 recurrent head-and-neck lesions treated micrographically reported 4.6% recurrence and a calculated 5-year cumulative re-recurrence probability of 2.9%. Box 10 states that micrographically controlled surgery shall be offered for high-risk BCC, including recurrent disease, aggressive subtypes, critical sites and indistinct margins (Grade of recommendation A; Level of evidence 1; consensus 100%).

document_sections.heading: 8.1.4. Procedure in the event of incomplete excision
document_sections.content: Incomplete removal means tumour remains at one or more surgical margins. Reported frequencies are 4.7–24% and vary with surgical experience, site, histological subtype and simultaneous removal of multiple lesions. A meta-analysis of 106,832 BCCs reported 11% incomplete excision overall and 6.2% among dermatologist-treated patients. Following incomplete excision, recurrence occurs in 26% to 41% during 2–5 years of follow-up; series dominated by morpheic BCC had the most recurrences. Re-excision finds no residual tumour in about half of initially margin-positive cases. Nevertheless, recurrence risk after a prior recurrence exceeds 50%, particularly when both deep and lateral margins are involved, and some incompletely excised tumours recur with more aggressive histology. Retreatment is suggested for aggressive, recurrence-prone disease, including micronodular or multifocal tumours, or involved deep margins, especially at midfacial or other difficult sites; 3D surgery should be considered in these circumstances. In staged 3D surgery, removal of a positive margin is intrinsic to the procedure. Tangential or extremely close margins should be treated as incomplete excision. Radiotherapy should be considered when complete surgical removal is unlikely; clinical observation could also be considered for non-aggressive trunk lesions measuring < 2 cm. Box 11 says incompletely excised lesions shall be re-excised, particularly high-risk lesions or those with involved deep margins (Grade of recommendation A; Level of evidence 3; consensus 100%).

document_sections.heading: 8.2. Destructive therapies
document_sections.content: Curettage, electrocautery (electrodesiccation), cryosurgery (cryotherapy), and laser ablation are options for low-risk superficial and nodular BCC. Curettage permits histopathological assessment; cryotherapy and laser ablation destroy the tissue needed for it. Curettage ± electrodesiccation is suggested for low-risk primary BCC, although no international agreement establishes an optimal protocol. Results depend strongly on tumour features, site, and operator skill. Reported 5-year recurrence ranges from 3% to 20%; rates are lower on the trunk and extremities and higher for facial, recurrent, or terminal hair-bearing-site BCC. A study of superficial BCC measuring < 1 cm found no significant differences between curettage with electrodesiccation and conventional surgery in complications, recovery, appearance, or satisfaction at three months. RCTs comparing cryotherapy with PDT, surgery, or radiotherapy reported recurrence from 6% at 1 year to 39% after 2 years. A single-centre randomised non-inferiority trial in non-facial superficial BCC measuring 5–20 mm found tumour clearance at 1 year of 95.7% with curettage alone and 100% with cryosurgery, but its non-inferiority analysis was inconclusive. In an RCT of 240 patients with limb or trunk sBCC, surgery outperformed cryotherapy and CO2 laser ablation; the difference between complete-response rates for CO2 laser and cryotherapy was not statistically significant. CO2, Er:YAG, and Nd:YAG lasers vaporise tissue water in full or fractional ablative modes. Settings influence efficacy, standard operating procedures are lacking, and studies—mostly of laser pretreatment before PDT—provide no long-term follow-up data. An RCT of 39 patients with small primary nodular BCC found more complete responses at 3 months and fewer local relapses at 12 months with Er:Yag laser plus AFL-PDT than with MAL-PDT. A study of long-pulsed Nd:YAG in 11 patients with nodular BCC or sBCC reported promising results, little scarring, and no long-term adverse events after a mean follow-up of 9 months (range 6–15 months). Another study of 102 primary or recurrent BCCs treated with Nd:YAG reported favourable clearance and recurrence findings assessed by OCT at 2 months and 1 year: lesions < 5 mm needed only one treatment, whereas larger ones generally needed additional sessions. Among 31 patients with non-aggressive BCC smaller than 16 mm on the trunk or extremities, long-pulsed 1064 nm Nd:YAG produced histopathological clearance in 90% of lesions at 1 month. Conversely, a study of 78 BCCs found incomplete clearance in 31% at 3 months after Nd:YAG, alongside many adverse effects and poor cosmetic results. The formal recommendation assigns Grade of recommendation C, Level of evidence 2 to curettage ± electrodesiccation and cryotherapy as possible alternatives for small, low-risk BCC; consensus was 100%. For laser treatment, the formal assessment states that evidence is insufficient to establish effectiveness: Grade of recommendation X, Level of evidence 4, with 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.3. Topical therapies
document_sections.content: Topical treatment should be considered for superficial or low-risk nodular BCC when patients decline surgery or patient-related circumstances make surgery unsuitable, including age, comorbidities, concomitant medicines, or logistical barriers. The two approved topical agents for sBCC are imiquimod 5% and 5% 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). A consensus-based statement also allows topical or destructive treatment for low-risk superficial and nodular BCC when surgery is declined or unsuitable; it is designated GCP, with 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.1. Imiquimod
document_sections.content: Imiquimod modifies the immune response and is indicated for sBCC in immunocompetent adults, applied once daily on five days each week for 6 weeks. A non-inferiority RCT in sBCC compared imiquimod 5% once daily on five days weekly for 6 weeks, 5% 5-FU twice daily for 4 weeks, and two MAL-PDT sessions separated by 1 week, with follow-up to 5 years. Estimated treatment success at 1 year was 83.4% with imiquimod, 80.1% with 5% 5-FU, and 72.8% with MAL-PDT; the study supported non-inferiority of 5% 5-FU and superiority of imiquimod 5% relative to MAL-PDT. Tumour thickness and adnexal extension did not appear predictive of sBCC treatment failure. At 5 years, tumour-free survival probabilities were 80.5% for imiquimod, 70.0% for 5% 5-FU, and 62.7% for MAL-PDT, supporting superiority of imiquimod 5% over both comparators for primary sBCC. Evidence for nodular BCC is limited: a systematic review found imiquimod-associated clinical clearance of 77.4%, histopathological clearance of 72.9%, and recurrence of 1.8% after an average follow-up of 13.0 months. In low-risk superficial and nodular BCC, a trial comparing imiquimod 5% once daily for 6 weeks for superficial lesions or 12 weeks for nodular lesions against excision found successful responses at 3 years from treatment initiation of 84% and 98%, respectively (p < 0.0001). At 5 years, clinical benefit persisted in 82.5% of imiquimod recipients versus 97.7% of surgical patients (p < 0.001), consistent with the 3-year findings. Moderate or severe local erythema, swelling, erosion, crusting, irritation, and itching are frequently reported; approximately 5% experience systemic flu-like symptoms. Imiquimod is a useful clinical alternative to surgery for single or multiple low-risk sBCC. Combinations with curettage or cryotherapy have been reported but require more investigation; for nodular BCC, they might be considered individually. The formal recommendation says topical 5% imiquimod should treat primary superficial and small nodular BCC: Grade of recommendation B, Level of evidence 1, 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.3.2. 5-Fluorouracil
document_sections.content: The antimetabolite 5-FU, in its 5% formulation, is licensed for sBCC at two applications per day for 3–6 weeks. Available efficacy studies lack long-term follow-up. An RCT comparing 5% 5-FU with imiquimod 5% and MAL-PDT found 5-FU inferior to imiquimod but non-inferior to MAL-PDT for sBCC after 3 and 5 years. Local adverse-effect rates resembled those of imiquimod, but flu-like symptoms were not observed. The formal recommendation says topical 5% 5-FU should be used for superficial BCC and records these comparative efficacy findings: Grade of recommendation B, Level of evidence 2, 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.4. Photodynamic therapy
document_sections.content: PDT combines topical 5-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) or MAL with visible-light illumination; the resulting reactive oxygen species induce apoptosis and selective tumour-cell necrosis. MAL cream and an ALA nanoemulsion are approved in Europe for low-risk superficial and nodular BCC. Treatment comprises two sessions 1 week apart. PDT with 5-ALA or MAL should be considered for small, non-aggressive superficial or nodular BCC with tumour thickness not exceeding 2 mm when surgery is unsuitable or contraindicated because of age, comorbidity, medication, or logistical difficulties. Morpheic, pigmented, and micronodular variants, and lesions in sites with high recurrence or deep-penetration risk such as the facial ‘H’-zone, should not receive PDT. In reported studies, MAL-PDT cleared 92−97% of sBCC at 3 months; recurrence was 9% at 1 year and 22% at 5 years. A real-life prospective head-to-head study reported cumulative tumour-free survival at 5 years for sBCC of 62.7% after MAL-PDT, 80.5% after imiquimod 5% cream, and 70.8% after 5-FU. With MAL-PDT for nodular BCC, 91% had clinical clearance at 3 months and 76% retained lesion clearance after 5 years. In comparisons with surgery, initial clearance for sBCC was 92% versus 99% and recurrence at 1 year was 9% versus 0%, respectively; for nodular BCC, recurrence at 5 years was 14% versus 4%, respectively, making MAL-PDT inferior to excision on that outcome. MAL-PDT and cryotherapy had equivalent sBCC clearance and no difference in recurrence at 5 years: 22% versus 20%, respectively (p = 0.86). PDT gave better cosmetic results than either surgery or cryotherapy. In non-aggressive superficial or nodular BCC < 2 cm, a comparison of ALA nanoemulsion gel and MAL found complete response at 12 months after the last PDT session in 93.4% and 91.8%, respectively, establishing non-inferiority (p < 0.0001). A Gorlin syndrome cohort of 33 patients with 138 lesions treated with topical or systemic PDT achieved local control in 56.3% of lesions at 12 months. Cosmetic results and patient satisfaction can be excellent, although pain or discomfort during illumination is the main adverse effect of conventional PDT. Fractionated illumination was proposed to permit tissue reoxygenation during unilluminated intervals. Fractionated ALA-PDT yielded better sBCC response than single PDT, 88% versus 75%, but at 5 years performed significantly worse than conventional two-stage MAL-PDT, 70.7% versus 76.5%. For nodular BCC, cumulative recurrence probability at 5 years was 2.3% after excision versus 30.7% after fractionated ALA-PDT preceded by debulking. Additional photosensitisers and delivery methods remain under investigation. The formal recommendation says 5-ALA- or MAL-based PDT with red light should treat superficial and low-risk nodular BCC and notes that PDT is less effective than imiquimod 5%: Grade of recommendation B, Level of evidence 1, 75% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.5. Combined therapies
document_sections.content: Combining modalities seeks complementary or synergistic effects and should be confined to situations unsuitable for standard treatment such as surgery. Partial destruction before MAL-PDT may improve cure in nodular or pigmented BCC. In nodular BCC, prior CO2, Er:YAG, or diode laser treatment or surgical debulking increased reported cure rates up to 92.9−98.9%. UltraPulse CO2 laser before the usual two MAL-PDT sessions produced 100% complete clinical clearance and a 97.1% recurrence-free rate over a mean follow-up of 32.2 months. CO2 laser followed by two/three MAL-PDT cycles gave better responses in BCC thinner than 2 mm, a 93.6% recurrence-free rate at 5 years, and 43% lower direct costs. One session of Er:YAG AFL-primed MAL-PDT produced complete response at 3 months in 84.2% versus 50% after two MAL-PDT sessions; recurrence at 1 year was 6.3% versus 55.6%, respectively. A small BCC case series combining contact cryotherapy after CO2 laser ablation and MAL-PDT reported complete responses without recurrence after 22 months. AFL-assisted delivery of cisplatin and 5-FU for low-risk superficial and nodular BCC produced complete clearance in 89% (17/19) at 6 months and 79% (15/19) at 12 months. Curettage to remove visible pigment followed by MAL-PDT yielded complete response in 76.2% of pigmented BCC and recurrence at 1 year in 19.1%. Debulking nodular BCC by curettage before imiquimod gave 96% clearance after an average follow-up of 36 months. An RCT found freedom from recurrence at 1 year in 86.3% after curettage plus imiquimod versus 100% after surgery for nodular BCC. PDT plus imiquimod has mainly been described in small series or case reports. In recurrent BCC, administering imiquimod after two PDT sessions increased the reported cure rate from 60% with PDT alone to 75%. Cryotherapy produced an 83% clinical response in imiquimod-refractory BCC. Cryotherapy between weeks two and five of imiquimod therapy, termed immunocryosurgery, achieved 95% efficacy in primary nodular BCC and a 91.4% tumour-free rate at 5 years. Neoadjuvant imiquimod before Mohs surgery significantly reduced tumour size and the surgical defect compared with vehicle, but may leave discontinuous tumour nests that impair margin assessment. After Mohs surgery for facial superficial or nodular BCC, adjuvant ALA-PDT was followed by recurrence in 1 of 84 lesions at 2 years. Evidence for combined treatment is low because most supporting reports involve small series, short follow-up, and/or off-label use.

document_sections.heading: 8.6. Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: Radiotherapy is an alternative to surgery and may be considered as initial treatment when surgery is declined, unsuitable because of locally advanced disease or comorbidity, impossible with curative intent, or likely to cause disfigurement or poor cosmetic results. Relevant locations include the eyelid, nose, and lip and large lesions of the ear, forehead, or scalp. A systematic review and network meta-analysis covering 40 randomised trials and five non-randomised studies of primary BCC with differing follow-up estimated recurrence at 3.5% after radiotherapy, compared with 3.8% after standard surgery and 3.8% after Mohs surgery. With appropriate doses, radiation-induced secondary skin cancer risk is described as negligible, but it and long-term appearance warrant consideration in younger patients. External beam options include surface/orthovoltage X-rays, electrons, and megavoltage photons; interstitial brachytherapy, surface brachytherapy, and electronic brachytherapy are alternatives. Selection accounts for lesion size, site, depth, team expertise, and local resources. Brachytherapy results are comparable to external beam treatment, while its rapid dose falloff spares surrounding tissue. Intensity-modulated brachytherapy can personalise dose distribution, particularly where anatomy complicates implant placement. Prescribed dose and fractionation must reflect the radiobiological properties of the chosen modality. Advanced lesions may receive megavoltage radiation at 60–70 Gy in 2 Gy fractions, five fractions per week; 45 Gy in 10 fractions or 54 Gy in 18 fractions are described as equi-effective hypofractionated schedules. Hypofractionation can give good cosmetic results, but the fraction size should account for site and functional and aesthetic effects. More prolonged fractionation appears to improve cosmesis and should be used for poorly vascularised or cartilaginous sites. The treatment volume must include visible tumour and an appropriate variable margin while sparing surrounding healthy structures where possible. A certified medical physicist should oversee dosimetry and technical aspects for definitive, adjuvant, and palliative treatment. Radiotherapy is generally safe but can cause transient acute dermatitis, rarely with erosion, and later depigmentation or telangiectasias. The authors suggest avoiding it in younger patients because long-term trophic risks are insufficiently characterised; when needed, the decision should be shared within a multidisciplinary tumour board. After resection with microscopic R1 or macroscopic R2 residual disease, radiotherapy may be considered if the tumour board judges neither observation nor wide re-excision preferable. The formal recommendation says radiotherapy shall be used when patients decline or are unsuitable for surgery: Grade of recommendation A, Level of evidence 1, 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 8.7. Electrochemotherapy
document_sections.content: ECT may be offered if surgery or radiotherapy is infeasible or contraindicated. Short high-voltage electrical pulses permeabilise tumour-cell membranes, allowing bleomycin or cisplatin to enter. Described advantages include strong local control, limited injury to normal tissue and adverse effects, and a favourable cost–benefit balance. Over the past 20 years, ECT has mainly been used for palliation of bleeding and tumour-mass symptoms. InspECT data report overall and complete response rates for BCC of 96% and 85%. In an InspECT registry study of 623 BCCs in 330 patients receiving bleomycin-ECT, 81% of patients had complete response after one ECT course. Skin ulceration occurred overall in 16%, with G3 in 1%; hyperpigmentation occurred overall in 8.1%, with G3 in 2.5%. At 17-month follow-up, 9.3% of patients had local recurrence or progression. A prospective RCT comparing ECT and surgery found no recurrence at 5 years in 87.5% of ECT-treated lesions and 97.5% of surgically treated lesions. ECT can treat locally advanced or recurrent BCC when standard options cannot be used, with good tumour control and functional outcomes and without systemic adverse events.

document_sections.heading: 9.1. Surgical therapy of laBCC
document_sections.content: Initial surgery for laBCC may struggle to achieve complete R0 removal and may entail major morbidity. Surgery nevertheless has a potential palliative role for problems such as uncontrollable tumour bleeding or intolerable pain. It may also follow neoadjuvant systemic therapy when tumour shrinkage permits a less extensive operation at a functionally sensitive site. Management should be planned by a skin-cancer multidisciplinary tumour board after full physical examination and Computed tomography-scan or MRI to assess invasion of bone, muscle, vessels, deep structures, or nerves. The formal consensus-based recommendation requires multidisciplinary decisions on whether surgery is suitable, indicated, and technically appropriate for laBCC; its designation is GCP, with 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 9.2. Radiotherapy of laBCC
document_sections.content: For laBCC, palliative radiotherapy can improve quality of life by relieving pain, bleeding, and ulceration. An accelerated hypofractionated short course delivers the total dose in fewer, larger fractions and can improve treatment adherence. External beam or interventional radiotherapy may also be proposed with curative intent: intensity-modulated and image-guided techniques offer precise delivery, strong local control, and relatively few adverse effects. Preliminary evidence encourages investigation of radiotherapy combined with HHI or immunotherapy, either neoadjuvantly or concurrently, because of possible synergy and the possibility of adapting radiation dose to clinical response.

document_sections.heading: 9.3. Hedgehog inhibitors
document_sections.content: Vismodegib and sonidegib inhibit Smoothened. Both have FDA and EMA approval for laBCC when surgery or radiotherapy is unsuitable; vismodegib is also approved for mBCC, whereas sonidegib has mBCC approval only in Switzerland and Australia. Oral doses are 150 mg/day for vismodegib and 200 mg/day for sonidegib. In the phase 2 ERIVANCE trial, vismodegib response rates for laBCC were 43% by independent review and 60% by site investigators; corresponding mBCC rates were 30% and 45%. Median response duration was 7.6 months and median progression-free survival 9.5 months in both cohorts. After 39 months of ERIVANCE follow-up, investigator-assessed overall response was 60.3% for laBCC, including 20 complete and 18 partial responses, and 48.5% for mBCC, all partial responses. Median response duration was 26.2 months for laBCC and 14.8 months for mBCC. Median overall survival could not be estimated for laBCC and was 33.4 months for mBCC. In STEVIE, investigator-assessed response after median follow-up of 17.9 months was 68.5% for laBCC and 36.9% for mBCC. In the pivotal BOLT sonidegib trial, the 200 mg daily dose yielded objective response after median follow-up of 13.9 months of 43% by central review or 67% by investigator review for laBCC, and 15% or 23%, respectively, for mBCC, under stringent modified RECIST criteria. Investigator review found response duration of 20.2 months and progression-free survival of 22.0 months. In BOLT’s final 42-month analysis, central-review response was 56% in laBCC and 8% in mBCC; median response duration was 26.1 months and 24.0 months, respectively, and median progression-free survival was 22.1 months (not estimable) for laBCC and 13.1 months for mBCC. Multiple BCCs in Gorlin syndrome should be regarded as laBCC and managed accordingly. Small Gorlin subgroups participated in ERIVANCE and BOLT; a separate multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial found significantly fewer new surgically eligible BCCs and smaller existing lesions with vismodegib than with placebo. A report of HHI reinduction in 12 patients with advanced BCC after failure of first-line HHI and second-line anti-PD1 treatment found complete or partial response in 33%, stable disease in 50%, and progression in 17%. Neoadjuvant HHI to shrink laBCC may be discussed, although randomised evidence of benefit is unavailable. In VISMONEO, 55 patients whose BCC was inoperable or operable only with major functional or aesthetic impact received vismodegib 150 mg/d for 4–10 months; surgery could be downstaged in 44 (80%). Radiotherapy could be combined with HHI and may be indicated after surgery for perineural invasion. Muscle spasms, taste changes, hair loss, fatigue, and weight loss occur in most HHI recipients and cause treatment discontinuation in approximately 30%. HHI trials reported no treatment-related deaths. Preventive and management approaches have been proposed to improve quality of life and benefit; treatment breaks or dose reductions have been considered for toxicity. The formal recommendation says HHI should be offered for laBCC or mBCC: Grade of recommendation B, Level of evidence 3, 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 9.4. Immunotherapy
document_sections.content: The rationale for anti-PD1 treatment in advanced BCC includes its exceptionally high TMB, its UV-associated immunogenic features, and BCC risk being 10 times higher in organ-transplant recipients and others with impaired immune surveillance than in the general population. These observations suggest laBCC and mBCC may respond to PD-1 antibodies. A pivotal single-arm, multicentre phase 2 study published in 2021 investigated intravenous cemiplimab (REGNONC 1620), a recombinant human IgG4 anti-PD-1 antibody, after progression on or intolerance of HHI. Eighty-four patients with laBCC received 350 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for up to 93 weeks, until progression, or until unacceptable toxicity. Independent central assessment found an objective response rate of 31%; 5 patients (6%) achieved complete response. Investigators reported neither unexpected BCC-specific adverse events beyond recognised anti-PD-1 effects nor treatment-related deaths. An laBCC update presented at EADO 2022 after 15.9 months of follow-up reported complete response in 7.1%, partial response in 25.0%, observed response duration of 85.2% at 6 months, and disease control of 79.8%. Median progression-free survival was 16.5 months, median overall survival had not been reached, and 80.3% were alive at 2 years; no new safety signals appeared. A presented and submitted primary analysis of 54 patients with mBCC from REGN-ONC 1620 reported 1 complete response (1.9%), 12 partial responses (22.2%), median response duration of 16.7 months, and median progression-free survival of 8.3 months. Median overall survival had not been reached; 84.4% were alive at 12 months. No new safety signals were reported, and tolerability resembled that in laBCC. The authors conclude that cemiplimab has clinically meaningful activity after HHI progression or intolerance, with safety broadly consistent with earlier cemiplimab and PD-1-inhibitor experience. FDA and EMA approved cemiplimab in 2021; it is described as the only approved PD-1 antibody for advanced BCC. The formal recommendation says anti-PD1 immunotherapy should be offered as second-line treatment after progression on HHI or when HHI is contraindicated: Grade of recommendation B, Level of evidence 3, 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 9.5. Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Evidence on systemic chemotherapy for mBCC comes only from case reports and case series. Most patients with widespread metastases received platinum-based treatment. Reported response was generally no higher than 20−30%, although rates up to 60% occurred occasionally; even in nearly all successfully treated cases, responses lasted no longer than 2–3 months. Chemotherapy might be considered for laBCC or mBCC that fails to respond or progresses after HHI and PD-1 inhibitors, either alone or with radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 9.6. Best supportive care
document_sections.content: Because advanced BCC frequently affects older patients, HRQoL should inform treatment selection and be reassessed throughout therapy; EORTC QLQ-C30 is among the tools used. Palliative care should address nutrition, psychological and social concerns, and existential needs, with specialist-team input and early conversations about individual wishes, needs, values, and future care. Deep or local infiltration can cause pain, ulceration, exudate, and odour, substantially affecting well-being. Pain should be checked regularly with validated tools, including the visual analogue scale, verbal rating scale, or NRS. A score exceeding 2 of 10 calls for discussion of pain. Chronic analgesics are preferably oral and scheduled regularly rather than only as required. The WHO three-step ladder progresses from paracetamol or NSAIDs to weak and then strong opioids according to pain; at intermediate (NRS 4) or severe (NRS 7) pain, immediate addition of tramadol, dihydrocodeine, or codeine to mild analgesia might be preferable. Surgery, radiotherapy, or ECT should be discussed for ulcerating or exuding tumours to control the lesion or ease symptoms. Radiotherapy is particularly useful for pain, haemorrhage, and extension towards critical areas such as the orbits. Daily washing with tap water or sodium chloride solution is mandatory for odour control. A review found evidence for topical metronidazole gel or solution at 0.75−0.8% once daily for at least 14 days, sodium chloride dressings, activated carbon dressings, and curcumin ointment. Metronidazole acts against anaerobes and protozoa and can also be taken orally at 500 mg three times daily for 10–14 days. Sodium-chloride-impregnated viscose or polyester dressings act through a hypertonic effect. In a randomised study, 0.2% polyhexamethylene biguanide eliminated malignant-wound odour by day 8 in all patients and was as effective as metronidazole 0.8% solution; odour control significantly improved general HRQoL. Zinc oxide paste or silicone gel on adjacent skin can prevent exudate-associated maceration. Calcium alginate, dressings with xylometazoline or adrenaline (1:1000), and silver nitrate can temporarily arrest bleeding. Depending on severity, bleeding management may use local haemostatic products or dressings, radiotherapy, endoscopic ligation or coagulation for gastrointestinal bleeding, or transcutaneous arterial embolisation. A formal GCP consensus statement recommends early involvement of an interdisciplinary best supportive care team for symptomatic laBCC or mBCC; consensus was 100%.

document_sections.heading: 10. Clinical trials
document_sections.content: Second-generation Hh-pathway agents under study include patidegib, saridegib (IPI-926), taladegib (LY2940680), and silmitasertib (CX4945). Topical patidegib 2% and 4% have reportedly reduced facial BCCs in Gorlin syndrome; a phase 3 study of 2% gel has been completed (NCT03703310). Silmitasertib (CX-4945), an ATP-competitive caseinkinase II inhibitor, is under investigation for laBCC or mBCC resistant to SMO inhibition (NCT03897036). Intralesional approaches are being studied for their potential to lower dose, increase local activity, and possibly reduce immune-related adverse effects relative to intravenous administration. Investigations include intralesional cemiplimab for BCC and cutaneous SCC (NCT03889912); oncolytic TVEC (NCT03458117) or RP-1 in organ-transplant recipients with cutaneous malignancy (NCT04349436); and L19IL2/L19TNF (Daromun/Fibromun), which links IL-2 or TNF to a human single-chain variable fragment directed at fibronectin’s extra-domain B, in trials including advanced BCC (NCT04362722, NCT05329792). Other intralesional candidates are the Emm55-encoding pDNA autologous cancer-cell vaccine IFx-Hu2.0 (NCT04925713), and nanoparticle-delivered siRNA STP705 directed at TGF-β1 and COX-2 in a phase II dose-escalation study (NCT04669808). ASN002, an adenoviral vector intended to deliver the human IFN gene into BCC cells for sustained local IFNγ, is being studied with vismodegib in phase II among patients with multiple sporadic BCCs or Gorlin syndrome (NCT04416516). Neoadjuvant trials include recruiting patients for phase 2 sonidegib followed by surgery or imiquimod (NCT03534947). Early data from 18 participants in an ongoing neo-BCC trial of TVEC, presented at ESMO 2022, suggested tumour shrinkage and improved operability in most. Pembrolizumab is under perioperative neoadjuvant/adjuvant assessment for resectable advanced head-and-neck BCC (NCT04323202). In unresectable advanced disease, a phase 2 study compares nivolumab plus ipilimumab or relatlimab after progression on nivolumab alone (NCT03521830); a single-centre phase II study combines intravenous cemiplimab with pulsed oral sonidegib on the expectation of synergy (NCT04679480). These interventions are described as research, not established recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 11. Follow-up
document_sections.content: BCC warrants follow-up because of local recurrence, further BCCs, and increased SCC and melanoma risk. Evidence does not establish better disease-burden or cosmetic outcomes from intensive surveillance of low-risk BCC. A recent study nonetheless supports tailoring information to each patient, and the authors consider one follow-up appointment reasonable for everyone to review diagnosis and treatment, counsel on sun protection, and explain self-monitoring for recurrence and new tumours. Recurrence risk varies by histopathological subtype, primary lesion size and location, and treatment; it is low for most guideline-treated primary BCC, but higher after recurrent disease, at high-risk facial sites, and with multiple lesions. Patients treated for recurrence should be advised to return if the previous treatment site changes. Most metachronous BCCs arise within the first 3 years after diagnosis, although excess risk persists. A meta-analysis found a pooled mean cumulative risk of subsequent BCC at 5 years of 36%, consistent with another observational study. Numerous primary BCCs beginning before age 30 years should prompt screening for Gorlin syndrome. Such patients also face other tumour risks and need discussion by an experienced multidisciplinary team, particularly as surgery may be unsuitable. A systematic review found follow-up recommendations inconsistent across BCC guidelines. Those previously treated for recurrent BCC and those with multiple BCCs appear to need more rigorous, longer-term review: every 12 months for 3–5 years, potentially lifelong. For difficult-to-treat or advanced BCC, a multidisciplinary team should determine individual follow-up frequency. A formal GCP consensus statement recommends risk-adapted follow-up at 3–12 monthly intervals for BCC, with 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 12. Diagnosis and management of patients with Gorlin syndrome
document_sections.content: Gorlin syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant familial cancer syndrome with high penetrance, variable expression, and estimated prevalence of one per 40,000–60,000 persons. It results chiefly from PTCH1 mutations; de novo mutations occur in 20−30% of patients. SMO, SUFU, and PTCH2 are less frequent causes. Diagnosis in a proband requires two major and one minor clinical criteria, or one major and three minor criteria. Major criteria are > 5 lifetime BCCs or BCC before age 30 years, lamellar calcification of the falx, jaw keratocyst before age 20 years, desmoplastic medulloblastoma, palmar or plantar pits, and a first-degree relative with Gorlin syndrome. Minor criteria comprise lymphomesenteric or pleural cysts, occipitofrontal circumference > 97th centile, cleft lip or palate, vertebral or rib anomalies on chest or spinal X-ray, preaxial or postaxial polydactyly, ovarian or cardiac fibromas, and ocular anomalies. Genetic testing should be performed selectively: prenatally where the familial mutation is known; to clarify suggestive but insufficient clinical findings and enable greater surveillance; or predictively in an at-risk relative who does not meet clinical criteria. Options include sequential PTCH1 or SUFU testing, a multigene panel, or broader genomic testing. Skeletal or dysmorphic radiological abnormalities occur in up to 60%, but investigations solely to establish criteria should be avoided when they have no therapeutic consequence, to minimise X-ray exposure. Close surveillance by a dermatologist skilled in dermatoscopy and skin-cancer detection is required for early BCC diagnosis and treatment. Examination of all skin, including scalp and genitalia, should begin annually at age 10 years for PTCH1-variant carriers and age 20 years for SUFU-variant carriers, then occur every 4–6 months. Except for radiotherapy, sporadic-BCC treatments may be considered according to lesion number, size, site, and subtype. Surgery’s benefit must be weighed against repeated or new lesions and should be limited to solitary high-risk BCC. Small or superficial lesions at low-risk sites outside the face may instead receive topical therapy and/or careful observation during follow-up. Radiotherapy must be avoided because X-rays can generate new BCCs. Multidisciplinary tumour-board discussion is needed for locally advanced disease. Emerging genotype–phenotype findings show significantly greater likelihood of medulloblastoma, meningioma, or ovarian fibroma with pathogenic SUFU than pathogenic PTCH1 variants. Skeletal abnormalities have been associated with more numerous and severe BCCs and other growths, including keratocystic odontogenic tumours and ovarian fibromas; more vigilant lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance beginning in childhood should be considered for these patients. Imaging is also recommended for associated extracutaneous abnormalities. Childhood brain MRI surveillance for medulloblastoma is justified with SUFU-related but not PTCH1-related syndrome. The Host Genome Working Group suggests annual assessment by a medical geneticist or clinician familiar with Gorlin syndrome to evaluate non-tumour manifestations, explain warning symptoms, and ensure screening occurs. Table 4 presents specialist-based screening and follow-up schemes for PTCH1 and SUFU variant carriers. Formal GCP consensus statements specify diagnosis by clinical criteria, with germline Hedgehog-pathway testing offered in selected cases, and require multidisciplinary treatment, with HHI considered for selected patients; both achieved 100% consensus.

document_sections.heading: 13.1. Sun protection and preventive measures
document_sections.content: Avoiding excessive natural or artificial UV exposure is central to primary BCC prevention because UV radiation has an established causal role. BCC development is strongly associated with the number of sunburns. Tanning-bed users have higher BCC risk than non-users, particularly when first use occurs before age 20 years. Shade, covering clothing, and sunscreen can reduce excessive sunlight exposure; tanning beds should be avoided. UV protection is particularly important for children and adolescents, people with sun-sensitive phototypes, personal or family skin-cancer history, immunosuppression, or prolonged occupational or recreational outdoor exposure. Because people diagnosed with BCC have increased risk of further skin cancers, all should be educated about avoiding excessive solar and sunbed UV exposure and maintaining regular skin surveillance.

document_sections.heading: 13.2. Chemoprevention
document_sections.content: Studies have suggested less BCC with a Mediterranean diet or high caffeine intake, but evidence does not establish a particular preventive dietary pattern. In an RCT meta-analysis, oral selenium, vitamin A, and beta-carotene did not reduce BCC incidence and cannot be recommended for that purpose. Vitamin D should be supplemented when deficient, especially with consistent comprehensive photoprotection; no additional preventive benefit against BCC has been proven. Nicotinamide, a water-soluble vitamin B3 (niacin) form, is thought to support repair of UV-damaged DNA and counter UV-related immune suppression. In a phase III RCT involving immunocompetent people with multiple previous skin cancers, oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months was associated with a 20% lower rate of BCC development; the effect appeared confined to treatment. The authors consider it a safe, inexpensive option worth considering for this high-risk group, but evidence is insufficient to recommend it for primary prevention in the general population. A 12 month placebo-controlled trial found that oral nicotinamide did not reduce BCC numbers in immunosuppressed solid-organ transplant recipients. Although oral retinoids are used to prevent SCC in high-risk patients, their low observed efficacy and benefit–harm balance do not support BCC prevention. A meta-analysis of 11 studies estimated 10% lower BCC risk with any NSAIDs (RR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.84–0.97]); the smaller inverse association for nonaspirin NSAIDs was not statistically significant (RR, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.86–1.02]). Associations were strongest in higher-risk people with actinic keratoses or previous skin cancer. Small effects, study heterogeneity, unanswered questions about dose, timing, drug type, and confounding, and possible cardiovascular harms of long-term NSAIDs prevent a recommendation for BCC chemoprevention. There is currently no evidence supporting topical tazarotene or tretinoin for primary BCC prevention.

document_sections.heading: 14. Communication with patients
document_sections.content: At diagnosis, patients should be told that BCC is generally locally invasive and does not impair survival except in rare advanced or high-risk cases, while also learning the consequences of leaving even a slowly growing lesion untreated. Surgery-related morbidity and the psychological effects of disfiguring operations merit discussion. Appropriate treatment choices should always be offered, particularly where referral to surgical rather than dermatological services changes which modalities are available. For older people with suitable low-risk BCC, curettage and cautery should be discussed as a way to avoid more invasive surgery involving flaps or grafts. Previous radiotherapy increases BCC risk within the treated field, chiefly low-risk and infundibolocystic lesions; repeat radiotherapy there is precluded by major-complication risk, so the history of irradiation at that site should be checked. Immunosuppressed patients with BCC need follow-up in dedicated clinics because their SCC risk is also high. Evidence concerning vitamin D intake remains debated; a recent meta-analysis was described as supporting serum vitamin D below 30–60 nmol/L as a balanced level. Patients should watch for both recurrent and new primary lesions: risk of a second BCC is 10 times that of the general population. Multiple primaries at presentation indicate greater relapse risk. Truncal BCC, especially superficial disease, is often followed by multiple new primaries within the first 5 years. Long-term surveillance is particularly likely to be needed with high-risk tumours or sites, multiple BCCs, or Gorlin syndrome. Patients with Gorlin syndrome often experience considerable anxiety about multiple skin cancers; although lesions begin young and may be numerous, they are usually less aggressive than sporadic BCC. When discussing HHI, clinicians should explain adverse effects and balance benefits and harms individually. Most treated Gorlin patients discontinue HHI within 6 months because substantial adverse effects, especially muscle cramps, are common and can be severe; these agents are therefore unlikely to provide a long-term solution, and intermittent schedules should be discussed openly. Non-surgical choices should be considered wherever possible and revisited at every appointment. Suspected Gorlin syndrome also warrants discussion of genetic testing. Families should know of their small increased risk of other rare cancers and the importance of taking unusual future symptoms seriously to enable earlier detection.
